name: ALEKS (Assessment and LEarning in Knowledge Spaces), McGraw Hill
origin_region: Global, US-origin. Grew out of NSF-funded research at the University of California, Irvine by Jean-Claude Falmagne and Jean-Paul Doignon; commercialised by ALEKS Corporation from the late 1990s and acquired by McGraw Hill. Now serves roughly four to five million students per year across mathematics, chemistry, statistics and accounting, in the US and internationally.
target_age: Core K-12 math band is grades 3-12 (the lowest classic course is 'Mathematics - LV 3', which covers Grade 3 state standards), plus higher education and college placement. In March 2024 McGraw Hill launched ALEKS Adventure, an AI-based game-framed extension for grades K-3 (grades 1-2 shipped for 2024-25, full K-3 for 2025-26). For an Indonesian SD context the relevant band is LV 3 to LV 6 plus ALEKS Adventure.
delivery_mode: online-app (browser-based; sold both as school/district licences and as a direct-to-family 'Independent Use' consumer subscription). No offline mode, no human tutoring component.
language_localization: No Bahasa Indonesia. ALEKS mathematics is fully English/Spanish bilingual - selecting the Spanish toggle (bottom-right of the Student Module) translates the interface, the explanations and the definitions, and ALEKS Adventure adds Spanish spoken audio. That bilingual build proves the platform is architecturally translatable, but Indonesian is not among the shipped languages, and an SD child would face English (or Spanish) word problems. Because ALEKS deliberately uses open-response word problems, a language barrier here directly corrupts the assessment signal.
pricing_model: subscription (consumer/homeschool tier, prices from McGraw Hill's official ALEKS K-12 subscription page): USD 19.95 for 1 month, USD 49.95 for 3 months, USD 99.95 for 6 months, USD 179.95 for 12 months. Family discounts apply when multiple students are bought in one transaction (e.g. 12-month: USD 305.90 for 2 students, USD 431.88 for 3, USD 539.84+ for 4 or more - up to about 44 percent off). School and district site licences are quoted separately. A subscription includes one Student Account plus one Master (parent) Account at no extra cost. At roughly IDR 320,000 per month this is priced well outside the mainstream Indonesian SD household.
local_curriculum_alignment: None for Indonesia. ALEKS course products are mapped to US state standards and Common Core (e.g. 'Mathematics - LV 3 provides comprehensive state standards coverage of Grade 3 Math'), with separate Canadian and higher-ed catalogues. There is no Kurikulum Merdeka or K13 mapping, no AKM alignment, and no Indonesian localisation programme found.
does_error_type_diagnosis: no - and this is now verified directly from ALEKS's own documentation and from the authoritative peer-reviewed account of its engine, not inferred. Knowledge Space Theory is a theory of WHICH items a student has mastered, not WHY a given response was wrong. The assessment output is a 'knowledge state': a subset of the domain's problem types (items) that the student most likely knows, plus the 'outer fringe' of items they are ready to learn next. Every item is resolved to one of three labels - in-state (likelihood above about 80 percent), out-of-state (below about 20 percent), or uncertain. There is no category for 'misread the question', 'holds misconception X', or 'arithmetic slip'. The check for a hidden error-type layer came back negative on all three probes: (a) ALEKS's own Knowledge Space Theory page and Research Behind ALEKS page never use the words misconception or error type; (b) the definitive technical paper (Cosyn, Uzun, Doble & Matayoshi, Journal of Mathematical Psychology, 2021) formalises response noise as exactly two scalar parameters per item - a careless error probability beta_q and a guessing probability eta_q - which are NOISE TERMS to be corrected for, never diagnostic outputs shown to anyone; (c) the wrong-answer path in Learning Mode serves a pre-authored 'Explanation' of how the problem should be solved for that problem type, i.e. a canonical worked solution, not a response to what this particular child did.
diagnosis_granularity: topic-mastery-map - but the finest-grained and most mathematically rigorous topic-mastery map in the entire competitor set, which is precisely why it is the sharpest available proof that a mastery map is not an error taxonomy. Granularity: a domain is decomposed into a few hundred problem types (about 400-500 core problem types for Algebra 1), and the combinatorial structure of feasible knowledge states is enormous (the College Placement knowledge structure contains roughly 10^23, about 2^77, states). ALEKS localises a student inside that structure in about 25-30 questions (initial assessment capped at 30, of which up to 29 are adaptively selected and one is a randomly chosen 'extra problem' used for validation). So the resolution is 'this child knows problem type #217 but not #218' - extremely fine on the WHICH axis, and completely silent on the WHY axis. Explicitly NOT mcq-distractor-mapped-misconception (ALEKS avoids MCQ by design) and NOT a full error-type taxonomy.
diagnosis_input_modality: free-response typed entry (open-ended answer input tools that mimic paper-and-pencil work: math palette, fraction/expression builders, graphing tools, calculator) plus one self-report channel - an 'I don't know' / 'I haven't learned it yet' button on every assessment question. Deliberately NOT mcq-distractor: the paper states plainly that 'the system avoids multiple choice formats'. There is no OCR of a photographed worksheet, no handwriting-stroke capture, no video or spoken explanation, and no capture of intermediate working - the student does the scratch work on paper and types only the final answer. This is the structural ceiling on ALEKS's diagnosis: the engine observes a final answer and a self-reported unfamiliarity flag, and nothing about the process that produced the answer, so it cannot classify error type even in principle. Notably, the free-response design does buy ALEKS one thing IXL and most MCQ platforms lack: because lucky guesses are near-zero, a correct answer is strong evidence of mastery - it defeats the guessing form of the correct-answer trap, but not the flawed-method-right-answer form.
ai_tutor_diagnosis_reliability: The state estimation is the best-validated adaptive assessment mechanism in this competitor set - and that only sharpens the point, because what is validated is mastery localisation, not error-type classification (of which there is none to validate). Validation design: every assessment includes a randomly selected 'extra problem' that is not used to update the state, so its observed correct rate can be compared against the model's prediction; across the dataset the extra-problem correct rate for an item tracks the lucky-guess rate eta_q on outer layers and 1 minus the careless-error rate beta_q on inner layers, confirming the Basic Local Independence Model's predictions - and also showing that beta and eta vary by knowledge-state layer rather than being constant, a known model limitation the authors flag. Documented failure modes relevant to us: (1) the 30-question cap means the assessment usually terminates before convergence, leaving 'uncertain' items excluded from the assigned state, so the initial state systematically UNDERESTIMATES the student's true state (ALEKS compensates by fast-tracking those items in Learning Mode); (2) a documented fatigue effect in long ALEKS assessments (Matayoshi et al. 2018); (3) careless errors are far more common than lucky guesses in ALEKS because items are open-ended, so a mastered item can still be answered wrong and be silently absorbed as noise - the child's slip is modelled away rather than reported to anyone; (4) the update after an incorrect response must be deliberately non-aggressive because of that careless-error rate, which is exactly why the 'I don't know' button had to be added as a workaround. In short: ALEKS knows careless errors exist, measures their rate precisely, and treats them as statistical nuisance rather than as diagnostic information for the teacher or parent.
evidence_quote: From Cosyn, Uzun, Doble & Matayoshi, 'A practical perspective on knowledge space theory: ALEKS and its data' (Journal of Mathematical Psychology, 2021): 'Note that, because of the probabilistic nature of the assessment procedure, this final state may contain an item to which the student gave an incorrect response. Such a response is regarded as due to a careless error. ALEKS items typically have open-ended answers, in the sense that the system avoids multiple choice formats and instead uses answer input tools that mimic what would be done with paper and pencil. As such, the lucky guess probability may be assumed to be very small.' And on the formal model: 'For each q in Q, there are two constants beta_q, eta_q in [0,1[, respectively called (careless) error probability and guessing probability at q' - the entire response-error model is two scalars per item, 'with no' further structure. On the output: assessment yields 'the precise and comprehensive description of an individual student's competence' plus 'the problem types that the individual is ready to learn next'. Note the noun throughout: problem types and states, never kinds of mistakes. From ALEKS's own Master Account page, the complete parent feature list: 'Change your name, address, or password'; 'Check your automatic payments'; 'Change your billing information'; 'Change the grade, topic, and password on your student account(s)'; 'View the progress and latest assessment report for each student account'.
how_parent_involved: gatekeeper plus dashboard-only, and skewed heavily toward administration rather than pedagogy. In the consumer 'Independent Use' product, every subscription creates a Student Account and a Master Account held by the parent. ALEKS's own description of the Master Account lists six capabilities, and four of them are account or billing administration (change name/address/password, check automatic payments, change billing information, add students under the family discount). Only two touch learning at all: change the grade/topic/password on a student account, and 'view the progress and latest assessment report for each student account'. What the parent therefore receives is a pie chart of mastered versus not-yet-mastered topics and a percentage complete. The parent is never told what kind of mistake the child made, never given a sentence to say to the child, and never handed a remediation script - because the system does not compute that information for anyone, teacher or parent. In the school channel the pedagogical reporting goes to the instructor, and the parent is closer to passive.
ai_tutor_directly_to_child: no. ALEKS has no conversational AI that talks to a child. The child-facing feedback loop is: attempt an item, and on a wrong answer see a Wrong Answer page and an 'Explanation' pop-up containing a pre-authored, structured walkthrough of how that problem type should be solved, after which ALEKS serves a fresh instance of the same problem type to re-test. That explanation is generated from the item, not from the child's response, so two children who fail the same item for completely different reasons receive identical text. ALEKS Adventure (grades K-3) adds a game world, a character (Digit the Dog) and spoken audio narration, and McGraw Hill markets it as 'AI-based', but the AI referred to is the KST adaptive engine, not a dialogic tutor; [uncertain] whether any 2025-2026 ALEKS release adds genuine conversational tutoring, since McGraw Hill announced further AI portfolio expansion in mid-2026.
key_finding: Verified directly against ALEKS's own documentation and the peer-reviewed specification of its engine: the claim holds exactly as stated, and the verification makes it stronger rather than weaker. ALEKS is the most mathematically rigorous student-model in commercial edtech - Knowledge Space Theory gives it a formally defined combinatorial structure of trillions of feasible knowledge states over a few hundred problem types, localised in about 25-30 open-response questions, validated against millions of assessments. And its entire output vocabulary is 'in-state / out-of-state / uncertain' per problem type. There is no hidden error-type layer. The most striking finding is what ALEKS does with error types it demonstrably knows about: careless errors are formalised as a per-item probability beta_q, empirically estimated at scale, shown to vary by knowledge-state layer - and then used purely as a noise correction inside the Bayesian update. The information 'this child probably slipped rather than failed to understand' exists inside ALEKS's mathematics and is deliberately discarded before it reaches any human. That is the market gap in its purest form: the industry's best student model treats error type as noise to be filtered, not as the product. Two secondary findings matter for our thesis. First, ALEKS's free-response-only design (explicitly refusing multiple choice) is the strongest existing commercial precedent for our own input choice, and it eliminates guessing as a confound - but because it captures only the final answer and not the working, it still cannot see a right answer reached by a wrong method. Second, on the parent axis ALEKS is weaker than IXL: the Master Account is predominantly a billing console with a progress view bolted on. Combined with English/Spanish-only localisation, USD 179.95 per year, and US-standards alignment, ALEKS is not a competitor for the Indonesian SD segment on either axis.
study_scale_or_sample: Very large. Platform scale: about four to five million students use ALEKS annually. The 2021 Journal of Mathematical Psychology paper analyses data from over 3.1 million initial assessments (2,688,472 of the College Placement assessments ran the full 29 adaptive questions), gives roughly 9,000 data points per item for the College Placement dataset, and draws on a base of 6,701,233 complete ALEKS learning-and-assessment profiles; the Algebra I analyses cover about 196,000 students, 77 percent of whom answered at least 20 questions. Independent efficacy synthesis: a 2021 meta-analysis in Investigations in Mathematics Learning (Sun & Else-Quest) pooled 56 independent effect sizes from 9,238 students across 33 studies of K-12 and higher education published between 2000 and August 2020.
evidence_strength: strong. The negative finding (no error-type diagnosis) rests on primary sources: ALEKS's own Knowledge Space Theory and Research Behind ALEKS pages, its Master Account page, its student/instructor manuals, and above all the peer-reviewed technical paper written by ALEKS's own research staff, which specifies the complete response-error model as two scalars per item. Multiple independent probes for a hidden misconception layer all returned nothing. Mechanism and documentation agree. The efficacy evidence is independent (peer-reviewed meta-analysis, not vendor-commissioned) and unusually candid.
remediation_efficacy_evidence: Mixed-to-weak, and importantly NOT a validation of diagnosis-driven remediation. The 2021 peer-reviewed meta-analysis (56 effect sizes, 9,238 students, 33 studies, 2000 to August 2020) concluded that ALEKS was as good as, but not better than, traditional classroom teaching - a very small positive effect on learning overall. An IES-funded efficacy study of ALEKS for improving student algebra achievement was run across ten schools in a large Pennsylvania metropolitan district. No What Works Clearinghouse rating or ESSA evidence tier for ALEKS was found in this search [uncertain]; McGraw Hill also cites internal ALEKS Adventure implementation results showing assessment-score gains, which are vendor-reported and not independently evaluated. The interpretive point for our gap thesis is sharp: ALEKS represents the most precise possible execution of the 'map exactly which skills are missing, then teach those' strategy, executed over two decades on millions of students - and independent synthesis says it merely matches ordinary teaching. That is indirect but real evidence that knowing WHICH skill is missing is not sufficient, which is the space an error-type diagnosis would have to earn its keep in. It cuts both ways for us: it is the strongest argument that the mastery-map paradigm has hit a ceiling, and simultaneously a warning that no commercial product has yet demonstrated that error-type diagnosis breaks through it.
